dataset.title: Dataset: 2015-2018 USA-MDA TMON Marsh Biomass Surveys
dataset.abstract: Biomass surveys conducted each fall from 2015 to 2018 at the Global Change Research Wetland (GCREW) marsh, Corn Island, Bear Neck Creek, and other tidal wetland sites located at the Smithsonian Environmental Research Center in Edgewater, Maryland. Biomass measurements include allometry and percent cover classes.
dataset.intellectualRights: This dataset is listed under a Creative Commons BY 4.0 and can be used with attribution. https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

section.title: Plot establishment
section.para: Transects were established at each site, and plots were placed at randomly determined intervals along each transect. At each plot, locations were taken using handheld GPS, and 1m x 1m sampling plots were established using PVC and fiberglass markers.

section.title: Vegetation Cover Sampling
section.para: Boundaries were set up in each 1m x 1m plot, and visual percent cover was approximated using the Braun-Blanquet cover class estimation (Braun-Blanquet 1932). The cover class approximations for each species in each plot were then converted to fractional cover, and treated as the midpoint value for data analysis. The relative cover classes of other environmental conditions such as bare ground, open water, wrack, dead biomass, and leaf litter, were also recorded.

section.title: Herbaceous Biomass Harvest
section.para: In one corner of each 1x1m plot, herbaceous biomass was harvested when Distichlis spicata and/or Spartina patens were present within a 10 X 10 cm subplot. We harvested all aboveground biomass, live or dead in the subplot. In the laboratory, live biomass of each species was separated. All dead biomass was combined into one category. Samples were dried for a minimum of three days at 60°C in a Grieve forced-air drying oven, then weighed to the nearest .01 grams.

section.title: Phragmites australis
section.para: Within each 1 m x 1 m plot, we counted living and dead Phragmites stems. We measured the height and diameter of four stems in each plot. Diameters were measured at two heights, the base and 40 cm from the base of the stem (sometime referred to as diameter at knee height, DKH).

section.title: Iva frutescens
section.para: Within each 1 m x 1 m plot, we counted the number of living and dead stems (defined as a shoot emerging aboveground). Based on the ratio of living and dead stems, the diameter, at 40 cm, of 5 stems were measured. Three diameter measurements were made on the type of stem (living or dead) that was present in the greatest number and two measurements were made on the other category. We measured the total height of the bush. We also made two measurements, at right angles to each other, of diameter of the crown.

section.title: Other species allometry
section.para: Within each 1 m x 1 m plot, we counted the number of living stems for species other than Spartina patens and Distichils spicata. We measured the heights and diameter of all stems of each species with a limit of eight stems per species. Diameters were measured at the base and 40 cm of each stem (diameter at knee height, DKH).

section.title: Calculating Total Biomass
section.para: For species harvested in the 10 X 10 cm subplot, we estimated total plot biomass (g) by multiplying the dry weights of each species by 100 to estimate biomass as grams per square meter. The biomass of litter in each 10 X 10 cm subplot was also converted to g m-2.

For species that were measured (diameter and height), we estimated biomass using the allometric equations published by Lu et al. (2016). Each function takes height as a mandatory input, and DKH as an optional input. The list of functions contains species-specific allometric equations for most of the species present, and generic grass and forb equations for the rest. In one case we applied the allometric equation for Iva frutescens to Morella cerifera because it was the only shrub-specific allometric equation available for the site.

For each herbaceous species in which biomass was estimated using allometry, we first calculated the average biomass of all stems measured, then multiplied average plant biomass by the number of stems counted in the 1 x 1 m plot to estimate biomass as g m-2.

For the shrub Iva frutescens, biomass was estimated for all shoots (living and dead) in each 1 m x 1 m plot. First, the biomass of the 5 separate shoots that were measured was calculated from the allometric equation for Iva. Second, the average biomass of the 5 shoots was calculated. Third, average shoot biomass was multiplied by the number of live shoots to calculate the biomass (g m-2) per plot.

section.title: Data Quality Control
section.para: After data had been scanned and digitized, datasets were inspected by an independent team. Edits were made to enforce site and transect naming consistency, and to correct typographical errors in species codes. We inspected summary statistics of cover percentages and corrected values that were out of bounds as described next. We plotted log-transformed distributions of width, diameter, and biomass for each species using box-and-whisker plots, and corrected some extreme high outliers (i.e. 3 x the interquartile range of the data) after comparing digital data to the original hand-written data sheets for data entry errors. We plotted changes in species biomass through time by plot and visually inspected trends to detect additional data entry errors. After cursory inspection and data visualization, we checked ~4% of the rows in the dataset against the original entry sheets. Out of 1,352 total entries, we found 6 true data entry errors, a 0.44% entry error rate. We judged that none of these were critical to calculating biomass by allometry.
